summary: Spokes ran its first Learning Festival, a pre-departure session at a Massachusetts DYS juvenile justice facility, where four riders taught 3D printing and berry-dye solar cell workshops. Students doubted the team would actually bike across the country.
learning_festival: DYS (Department of Youth Services) juvenile justice treatment facility in central Mass (Westborough per the Day 0 post); workshops on 3D printing and berry-juice solar cells (TiO2 slides, iodide, multimeter tests); arranged through TEJI (MIT Educational Justice Initiative) and run with CES (Collaborative for Educational Services)
contacts: Prof. Lee Perlman, MIT TEJI (Educational Justice Initiative)
DYS facility, central Massachusetts
CES (Collaborative for Educational Services), MA
planning_notes: Juvenile justice facilities work as LF venues. This connection came through MIT's TEJI program (Lee Perlman), so ask inside-out program faculty and alumni first.
Berry-dye solar cells: raspberry and blueberry worked best; a competition kept students engaged. Winning cell measured 0.47 V with a flashlight and multimeter.

summary: Day one: the team left the Lincoln Memorial and rode the East Coast Greenway and busy Virginia roads toward Stafford, VA (about 58 miles planned). Sophia got leg cramps in the heat and rode in the support car for the rest of the day.
slept_at: Warmshowers hosts Lauren and Steve, Stafford VA (basement, laundry)
contacts: Lauren and Steve (Warmshowers hosts), Stafford VA
planning_notes: Electrolytes from day one: Nuun tablets (bought at Target) ended the leg cramps. Drink one plain water and one electrolyte bottle.
95 F with a water shortage: add more bottle cages to the bikes early on. A collapsible 5-gallon water jug (bought at REI) was used for the car.
East Coast Greenway out of DC has cold water fountains, but the route leaves the river breezes for busy roads and brutal hills near Stafford, VA.

summary: Day 2: on Virginia backroads a sudden thunderstorm forced the team to huddle until the Mineral Volunteer Fire Department truck picked them up, and a replacement bike rack was bought from a shop about an hour away. Day 4 was a rest day at a lake, then dumpling night at a host's home in Charlottesville.
slept_at: Mineral Volunteer Fire Department, Mineral VA (kitchen available, Day 2); Andrew's home, Charlottesville VA (Day 4)
contacts: Tom, Mineral Volunteer Fire Department, VA (picked the team up in a storm; hosted them for the night)
Andrew, Charlottesville VA (host, with Vonnie and Johnathon)
planning_notes: Mineral VA: the volunteer fire department hosts cyclists overnight and has a kitchen. Ask in advance.
A thunderstorm on rural backroads with no shelter: call a local contact for a pickup early rather than waiting it out on the road.
The bike rack needed replacing; the shop about an hour away was nearly closed when the team arrived. Call ahead for hours.

summary: First Learning Festival on the road, at the Louisa County Public Library in Virginia, with 3D printing, music, leaf chromatography, circuits and solar cell workshops. The library coordinator then recommended a soft-serve stop, and the team stayed with a friend of Sophia's in Charlottesville.
slept_at: Andrew's home, Charlottesville VA (friend of Sophia's)
learning_festival: Louisa County Public Library, VA; coordinator Ophelia; workshops on 3D printing, music, leaf chromatography, circuits and solar cells; lunch break with Frisbee and Museum outside
contacts: Ophelia, learning festival coordinator, Louisa County Public Library, VA
Andrew, Charlottesville VA (host)
planning_notes: Ask the LF coordinator for a post-event food stop. Ophelia's soft-serve suggestion became the team's post-LF ice cream tradition.
Louisa County Fire Station gave the team floor space the night before (see the Day 2 post).

summary: Left Charlottesville for Loft Mountain Campground in Shenandoah National Park, a 3,717 ft gain. Paved country roads turned into steep gravel and bushes, then a long Skyline Drive climb and a final steep mile, with a driver meeting them at a halfway picnic table.
slept_at: Loft Mountain Campground, Shenandoah National Park, VA
planning_notes: The Loft Mountain approach is brutal: a gravel road into Shenandoah, a long Skyline Drive climb, then a final 1-mile steep road. The 3,717 ft gain was far more than the team expected from the route plan.
The team's driver met them at a halfway picnic table near a stream. Plan a driver meeting point on long climb days.
Pack food and gear carefully: lunch and oat milk were left at the host's home and had to be retrieved by car.

summary: Breakfast with host Pam (grits and biscuits), then 45 miles to Lexington, VA. The team hit very steep climbs for about 10 miles after a ski shop stop, then rode wet switchbacks in rain and a long descent on Bike Route 76 before arriving at Dirk and Chrissie's home.
slept_at: Dirk and Chrissie's home, Lexington VA (Warmshowers host)
contacts: Pam (host, Virginia; town not stated)
Dirk and Chrissie (Warmshowers hosts), Lexington VA
planning_notes: The ~10 miles of steep climbing after the ski shop stop were the steepest of the trip so far. Plan extra time and rest before them.
Wet switchbacks on a mountain descent in rain are treacherous. Ride the descent carefully.
Tortilla-and-sardine lunches were the staple. Carry enough food for long climb days.

summary: Rode 55 miles from Lexington to Roanoke, VA, on the Chessie Nature Trail (gravel) and Bike Route 76, which avoided the Shenandoah climbs. A storm at the Buchanan Swinging Bridge led to two car shuttle trips, and the team cleaned and lubed their chains in Roanoke.
slept_at: Roanoke VA host family home (names not stated)
contacts: Dirk and Chrissie, Lexington VA (host; breakfast)
Roanoke VA host family (names not stated)
planning_notes: Chessie Nature Trail (gravel, out of Lexington VA) avoids the Shenandoah climbs. A Warmshowers host recommended it. Bike Route 76 after it had almost no cars.
Buchanan Swinging Bridge (VA) is a good lunch and swim stop, but when storms roll in, use a car shuttle. The team needed two trips (about 35 min drive).
Degrease and lube the chains at a host's home when you have spare time.

summary: Longest ride so far at 78 miles, from hosts Curtis and Jennifer through Trans America Trail (US Bike Route 76) signs and roads beside the interstate, with a cemetery lunch, ending in Abingdon, VA at Warmshowers host Julia's home.
slept_at: Julia's home, Abingdon VA (Warmshowers host)
contacts: Curtis and Jennifer (hosts; have hosted nearly 100 guests since 2019, including Spokes 2019)
Julia (Warmshowers host), Abingdon VA
planning_notes: 78-mile day: US Bike Route 76 signs guided most of the route, then it diverged onto local roads beside the interstate.
Abingdon VA has a walkable downtown with shops and a barbecue dinner with live music, a good reward after a long day.
Ask hosts for route advice. Curtis and Jennifer gave useful route tips for the next stretch.

summary: Rode 70 miles from Abingdon to Breaks Interstate Park on the VA/KY border. A lunch stop turned into a free potluck with a Tiller family reunion, and the final approach to the campground was uphill the whole way.
slept_at: Campground at Breaks Interstate Park (2 nights)
contacts: Tiller family (reunion at Council Park, VA; shared potluck leftovers)
planning_notes: Elevation maps understate the climbs: a hill that looked small on the phone was hard in person, and the 'flat' stretch was not flat.
The final approach to the Breaks campground is uphill the whole way. Pace it after a 70-mile day.
Council Park and Pool was the planned lunch stop, with a picnic shelter and playground.

summary: Rest day at Breaks Interstate Park: visitor center, a 0.35-mile geological hike, and a swim at the Russell Fork River in Kentucky. The team gave water to a lost couple on the trail and had a campfire that night.
slept_at: Breaks Interstate Park campground (second night)
contacts: Jason, local boy at the Russell Fork River, KY (shared his family's picnic food)
planning_notes: Russell Fork River (short drive into KY from Breaks) is a cold-water swim spot good for a rest day.
Carry extra water on trails. The team helped a couple at risk of dehydration after they lost the trail.

summary: Rode 41.7 miles from Wayland, KY to Hazard, KY with no incidents, stopping for a long break on the way. The team stayed with Wayland's mayor and his wife, then slept in a duck-themed room in Hazard.
slept_at: Duck-themed room in Hazard KY (likely the Mother Goose B&B the post names)
contacts: Jerry Fultz, mayor of Wayland KY, and his wife King (hosts; breakfast and a tour of the old high school gym)
Franklin's cousin, Paintsville KY (Chinese dinner and family visit)
planning_notes: Dogs chase riders in eastern Kentucky. The team bought air horns to deter them.
Wayland KY is tiny (about 400 people). The mayor gives out his cell number and hosts cyclists. Small-town officials can be good local contacts.

summary: Ran two days of workshops at the Hazard, KY Challenger Center (solar cells from berry juice for middle schoolers), plus the county fair. On June 17 they rode to the Red River Gorge area, waited out a thunderstorm in a church awning, and sheltered at a campground when the rain came.
slept_at: Harmony House Victorian B&B, Hazard KY (June 15 night); campground near Red River Gorge (later named Lota.Rocks campsite; owners let them shelter in the restroom building)
learning_festival: Challenger Center, Hazard KY (the first Challenger Center in a rural area); two days of workshops, solar cells from berry juice, for middle schoolers; Tom Cravens gave a control room tour
contacts: Tom Cravens, Hazard KY (arranged the Hazard LF)
Harmony House Victorian B&B, Hazard KY (host)
Dean, director of the Kentucky School of Traditional and Bluegrass Music, Hyden KY
planning_notes: Solar cell workshop for middle schoolers: they had not had chemistry yet. Conjugated-bond theory came too early. Start with the hands-on work.
Solar cell layers are thin, so fingerprints ruin them. Plan for careful handling and spare materials.
Miguel's pizza (Red River Gorge area) was recommended by four separate people. Make-your-own pizza.
Campground in the Red River Gorge area: owners let riders wait out a storm in the restroom building, which had ping-pong tables.

summary: Rode 68 miles from Red River Gorge to Lexington, KY on a cooler 74 F day after a heat wave. Dogs chased the team, and on the suburban roads into Lexington they witnessed a hit-and-run scene before police arrived. They stayed with church-group hosts Tony and Lynda.
slept_at: Tony and Lynda's home, Lexington KY (church-group host)
contacts: Tony and Lynda (church-group hosts), Lexington KY
planning_notes: Air horns are very loud and can ring your ears. Franklin thinks the noise may make dogs chase harder. Treat a horn as a backup, not a plan.
An early-June heat wave in Kentucky made it feel like 104 F. The cooler 74 F day felt much better, so plan the hardest days around heat.
Kentucky roads had many motorcycle groups (10+ groups, one with about 100 bikes). They waved and stopped traffic at intersections.

summary: Rode 63.79 miles from Lexington to Liberty, KY, with a park lunch of barbacoa burritos and Father's Day calls. Don and Cindy Cravens hosted a big dinner, then their family gave a farm tour, and the night ended with geodes in a fire pit.
slept_at: Don and Cindy Cravens' home, Liberty KY (women); Lewis and Ellen's home, Liberty KY (men)
contacts: Don and Cindy Cravens (Liberty KY; dinner and home stay)
Lucas and Bonnie, Liberty KY (gave the cow field tour)
Lewis and Ellen, Liberty KY (hosted the men)
Tom Cravens (arranged the short-notice Liberty stay)
planning_notes: Short-notice lodging worked through a personal network: a relative of Tom Cravens in Liberty KY found housing on very little notice.
Liberty KY is about 15 miles from the EDT/CDT time-zone border. Plan calls and pickups with the local 'fast time' and 'slow time' in mind.

summary: Rode 90 miles from Liberty to the Mammoth Cave campsite in roughly three 30-mile sections, in heat near 95 F. An Amish family fixed a flat on the way, and the team refilled water at gas stations.
slept_at: Campground near Mammoth Cave, KY
contacts: Don Cravens (Liberty KY; breakfast host; former superintendent)
Amish family on a KY backroad (Jethro, about 14, fixed the flat)
planning_notes: 90-mile day: split it into three roughly 30-mile sections with breaks. Refill water at gas stations during 90+ F heat.
On rural Kentucky two-lane roads, long lines of cars struggled to pass. Pull over now and then to let traffic through.
A flat was fixed quickly by an Amish family on a KY backroad. Local help is available on rural roads.

summary: Visited Mammoth Cave (55 F inside) and the Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, then rode 30.8 miles on hot farm roads to a hotel in Bowling Green. Berries were bought at a Kroger for the next day's solar cell workshop.
slept_at: Hotel in Bowling Green KY (name not given)
learning_festival: Solar cell workshop prep: berries bought at a Kroger in Bowling Green for the next day's LF
planning_notes: Mammoth Cave tours: the cave stays at 55 F year-round, so bring a jacket even in summer. The gift shop sells sweaters.
Bowling Green's Corvette Museum sits over the Mammoth Cave network. A 2014 sinkhole swallowed eight cars, and the museum now has a karst exhibit.

summary: Ran the Bowling Green, KY learning festival at WKU's Innovation Campus, which got local TV and newspaper coverage. Then rode 50.7 miles to Hartford, KY, where hosts Sharilyn and Tony had a pool and a bourbon tasting.
slept_at: Sharilyn and Tony's home, Hartford KY (pool)
learning_festival: WKU Innovation Campus (a former mall now housing startups), Bowling Green KY; set up by Sam Ford; workshops filmed by WBKO and WNKY
contacts: Sam Ford (MIT alum; set up the Bowling Green LF and drew local press)
Sharilyn and Tony (hosts), Hartford KY
planning_notes: A local contact can drive press: Sam Ford's outreach got two TV stations to film the workshops.
Post-LF tradition: GADS (Great American Donut Shop) in Bowling Green is open 24/7, as recommended by a local.
Lunch breaks ran long. The team agreed to shorten them; a community pool made one long lunch worth it.

summary: Rode 62.9 miles from Hartford to Henderson, KY through corn fields, chicken-farm country and Owensboro's bike paths, with a fried chicken lunch at a nature park. Stayed with hosts Karen and Roy in a cabin in Audubon Park.
slept_at: Karen and Roy's cabin, Audubon Park, Henderson KY
contacts: Karen and Roy (Henderson KY hosts; brought a keyboard for Robert)
planning_notes: The McDonald's near Hartford was the only breakfast restaurant in the area. Plan to bring breakfast food in western Kentucky.
Chicken-farm country: there was a strong ammonia smell and a steady stream of poultry trucks on the road.
Owensboro has bike paths and a nature park with gravel trails. Good lunch stop.

summary: Rode from Henderson, KY across the Ohio River into Illinois. Lunch at Fiedlerland RV Park in Old Shawneetown, then Warmshowers hosts Sherie and Brad in Harrisburg, who had biked Oregon to Maine the year before, fed the team watermelon and sourdough.
slept_at: Sherie and Brad's home, Harrisburg IL (Warmshowers)
contacts: Tim, Fiedlerland RV Park & Campgrounds, Old Shawneetown IL (has run it for 9 years)
Sherie and Brad (Warmshowers hosts), Harrisburg IL; biked Oregon to Maine the previous summer
planning_notes: Fiedlerland RV Park & Campgrounds (Old Shawneetown IL, across the Ohio River) is a lunch stop. Its sharpie-signed wall shows visitors from about 35 states.
Wide road shoulders on Kentucky and Illinois roads made long-distance riding comfortable.

summary: Rode 51 miles from Harrisburg to Murphysboro, IL, after waiting out morning thunderstorms and leaving around 2 PM, the latest departure of the trip so far. Stayed with Terry and Linda, Beatles fans with a pool that has a diving board.
slept_at: Terry and Linda's home, Murphysboro IL (friends of host Brad; pool with diving board)
contacts: Terry and Linda (Murphysboro IL hosts; spaghetti dinner)
Sherie (Harrisburg IL host; rode a few miles with the team)
planning_notes: Storm delay: the team waited out the morning thunderstorms and left at 2 PM. Build slack into the schedule for weather.
Bone-conduction headphones (bought at REI) let riders hear traffic. Shared Bluetooth earbuds lose their connection on switchback roads, so each rider needs their own pair.

summary: Rode 44 miles from Murphysboro, IL to Perryville, MO, with a lunch stop in Chester, IL and a crossing of the Mississippi into Missouri. Learned the host lived in a St. Louis suburb, which turned the next day into a 97-mile ride. The team decorated their car with chalk markers.
slept_at: Fraser and Elizabeth's home, Perryville MO
contacts: Fraser and Elizabeth, Perryville MO (hosts; instant pot pasta, S'mores, gem art)
Terry and Linda, Murphysboro IL (breakfast host)
planning_notes: Confirm the host's address before the ride. This host lived about 27 miles past the planned destination in a St. Louis suburb, which turned a 70-mile day into a 97-mile day.
Clean the chains when they get grimy. Chains went unwashed from Virginia until here, so do it at a host's home.
For group photos: prop the camera on a guardrail and use a 10-second timer. Riders can end up in the background if the driver drives by.

summary: The day before departure, the team ran a Learning Festival at a DC youth rehabilitation center (Maya Angelou Academy, with DYRS and YSC). It was also a scramble: members were still arriving, the bike rack was broken, and driver registration at Budget was still pending.
learning_festival: Youth rehabilitation center in DC (Maya Angelou Academy school program with DYRS and YSC); marker chromatography (black marker = teal and pink pigments) and a 3D-printed CF lung model; Judge Faruqui bought bagel lunches
contacts: Judge Zia Faruqui, DC district court (connected the team to the DC center)
Lee Perlman, MIT EJI (suggested expanding LFs to youth rehab centers)
Maya Angelou Academy, DYRS, and YSC (DC)
planning_notes: Don't schedule the last LF on departure eve. Rider arrivals, a broken rack and Budget driver registration all landed on one day.
Marker chromatography (black marker splits into teal and pink) was the favorite activity with this group.
Youth rehab center LFs were set up through a judge and MIT's TEJI network, not a cold outreach.

summary: Rode 92 miles from Perryville, MO to Chesterfield, MO, a St. Louis suburb, in three sections. A flat from road debris, a gravel road being repaved that forced a walk downhill, and a noisy highway shoulder for the last stretch.
slept_at: Noah's home, Chesterfield MO (family dog Moca)
contacts: Fraser Head, Perryville MO (host; breakfast before departure)
Noah, Chesterfield MO (host)
planning_notes: Google Maps sent the team onto a gravel road being paved near Perryville, MO. The surface was loose and a steep downhill had to be walked. Check the surface before trusting the route.
Road debris (a glass base with a spike) caused a flat. Carry a spare tube, patch kit and levers.
Google's 2-hour option for the last 30 miles to Chesterfield was a noisy highway shoulder, versus a 3-hour option. Check the shoulder before you commit.
Water bottle filling is a weekly role. Doing it as a pipeline during breakfast kept departure quick.

summary: Rest day in St. Louis: City Museum, the Arch, the Delmar Loop and Washington University. The next day ran the sixth Learning Festival at a Ferguson middle school summer program (the post says Ferguson, MI, but it is in the St. Louis area), then a potluck with host Noah.
slept_at: Noah's home, Chesterfield MO (night of June 30; June 29 night not stated)
learning_festival: Ferguson Middle School summer program for a gifted group; three class periods with three rotating workshops (3D printing, CAD, with an Among Us impostor design)
contacts: Noah and church friends (potluck host), Chesterfield MO
Ferguson Middle School, Ferguson (summer program)
planning_notes: For gifted middle schoolers, 3D printing theory was above the group's heads. A CAD workshop where kids design something of their own worked better.
Pappy's Smokehouse in St. Louis is lunch-only. Check hours before planning dinner there.

summary: Fourth of July rest day at Lake of the Ozarks, MO: caving at Ozark Caverns to escape the heat, then a swim at the lake. The next day was the first century, 105 miles from the lake to Springfield, MO (the post says MI). A bumpy gravel road, a broken pump and long rolling hills pushed them to a 9 PM arrival at barber and cyclist Greg's home.
slept_at: Lake of the Ozarks campground (July 4); Greg's home, Springfield MO (July 5)
contacts: Greg (barber and touring cyclist), Springfield MO (gave riding tips)
planning_notes: Early-July heat in Missouri came with a severe heat warning. Caves held at 56 F were an effective break. Caves need a 2-hour decontamination before you go into another cave (white-nose fungus).
The century started at 7 AM and ended at 9 PM, about 8 hours of riding. Start earlier to beat the heat.
A gravel road out of the lake shook the bikes, so the team let air out of the tires. The pump then broke, and the SAG wagon brought a replacement. Carry a backup pump.
